claims.text: This is a shojin-ryori (Buddhist vegetarian) kitchen, not a dedicated gluten-free one. Handmade soba (buckwheat noodles, which in Japan are commonly cut with wheat flour) is a core part of the menu, so wheat is regularly handled in the kitchen and a celiac should not assume the soba is safe.

Set meals include items seasoned with miso and soy-based sauces (for example konnyaku with a dark miso sauce and white-miso preparations). These typically contain wheat, so dishes are not inherently gluten-free; an adapted plate would need to be requested and confirmed in advance.
Dishes here rely on soy sauce and miso, the bulk of which in Japan is brewed with wheat. Assume soy sauce and miso contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.
The menu is largely vegan, but a diner reported that one side dish contained dashi (fish stock) and had to request it be removed, so not every plate is vegan by default.

Reports conflict on stock: a more recent review and on-site signage state the food is fully vegan with no fish stock and no animal ingredients, while an earlier report flagged dashi in a side. Confirm fish-stock use when ordering rather than relying on the menu's vegan framing.
Dairy is present for some items: milk is used for drinks, and the ice cream desserts are not vegan. Stick to the shojin sets and noodle bowls and skip the ice cream for a vegan meal.
Staff speak some English and accommodated a request to remove a dashi-containing side dish, suggesting requests can be made, though you should be explicit about needs.

An entirely meat- and fish-free shojin-ryori menu, which removes many cross-contact risks that come with mixed kitchens, making it a comfortable choice for vegetarians and a strong starting point for vegans who confirm stock and dairy.

name: 焼鳥 雷 本店 (Yakitori Kaminari – Honten)

claims.text: This is a charcoal yakitori shop where many skewers are basted in tare (a sweet soy-based sauce), and skewers are grilled together over a shared fire, so cross-contact between tare and salt-grilled items on the same grill is likely. It is not confirmed gluten-free safe; a celiac diner should treat it with caution and confirm directly.

The standard tare sauce used to baste skewers is soy-sauce based, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Salt-grilled (shio) skewers avoid the tare entirely and are the safer choice, but should still be confirmed with the grill master, who prepares everything himself.

The menu is built around grilled chicken and other meat skewers, with only a few non-meat items such as asparagus skewers (which are typically wrapped with chicken). There are no documented vegan or vegetarian options, and any vegetable skewers are grilled over the same charcoal as the meat, so cross-contact is unavoidable. Not suitable for vegans.
Because it is a single owner-operator doing all the prep and grilling, you can speak directly to the person handling your food and ask for shio (salt) preparation to avoid the soy-based tare.

This is a traditional yakitori-and-fried-food izakaya and is not a safe choice for celiac diners. Yakitori is typically brushed or dipped in tare (a sweet glaze built on soy sauce, which almost always contains wheat), and shared grills and fryers make cross-contact with wheat very likely. No gluten-free option has been documented here. Confirm directly with staff before relying on anything.

Yakitori tare and dipping sauces are built on Japanese soy sauce, which is normally brewed with wheat. Even salt-seasoned (shio) skewers are not a guarantee of being gluten-free given shared grilling surfaces.

The menu centers on grilled chicken skewers and fried dishes, so there is no vegan offering. Any vegetable item would be cooked on the same grill and in the same oil as meat and is not free of animal cross-contact.

name: 辛麺屋 鯱輪 京都今出川店 (Karamenya Shachirin Kyoto Imadegawa)

claims.text: Bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles in a shared spicy-ramen kitchen; no gluten-free preparation is mentioned (per Leaf Kyoto).
The menu includes a soy-sauce ramen and a chili-based spicy tare; Japanese soy sauce and chili tares are typically wheat-containing, though the page does not list allergens (per Osumituki).
Signature bowls are topped with stir-fried minced meat, seared chashu pork, back fat and a beaten egg over a meat broth; no plant-based option is offered (per Leaf Kyoto).

name: COFFEE Cattleya （コーヒーカトレヤ）【旧店名】祇園喫茶 カトレヤ (COFFEE Cattleya (Coffee Katoreya / Gion )

claims.text: This is a coffee house centered on toast, cake and light cafe fare, all of which involve wheat. Wheat is heavily present in the kitchen and cross-contact is highly likely, so the food menu is not celiac-safe.

No vegan options or dairy-free preparation are documented. Menu items center on coffee, espresso drinks, toast and cake; lattes and baked goods use dairy, and vegan suitability would need to be confirmed directly with the shop.
Black brewed coffee and espresso (Americano) without milk are plausibly free of gluten and animal products, though this is not confirmed by any source and should be verified with staff.

This is a classic yoshoku (Japanese-Western) restaurant whose core dishes are wheat- and soy-heavy: Fukuya Rice is built on ketchup rice with an omelet, and the menu centers on hamburg steak, breaded and fried cutlets (chicken cutlet), cream croquettes and a fried-item bento. Breading, demi-glace and similar sauces, and typical Japanese seasonings all generally involve wheat flour and soy-based sauces. No gluten-free preparation, dedicated fryer, or allergy accommodation is documented in any source, so this is not suitable for strict gluten avoidance and not vegan-friendly. Confirm any dietary needs directly with the restaurant.

This is a traditional Western-style (yoshoku) kitchen built around wheat-heavy dishes. Signature items include breaded, deep-fried cream croquettes (with a flour-based bechamel filling), shrimp fry, fried white fish, and chicken cutlet, all of which are coated in wheat flour and breadcrumbs and fried.
The hamburger steak is served in a demi-glace cream sauce; demi-glace and roux-style yoshoku sauces are typically flour-thickened. Not suitable for celiac diners.
Fried items and breaded foods share the same fryer in a small one-cook kitchen, so cross-contamination of any non-fried item with wheat is very likely. No gluten-free accommodation is indicated.

Sauces and dressings are homemade with no published ingredient lists; standard Japanese soy sauce (which usually contains wheat) is a common base in yoshoku sauces. Assume gluten is present unless confirmed otherwise with the owner.

No vegan or vegetarian options are indicated. The menu centers on meat, fish, fried foods, demi-glace/cream sauces, and homemade mayonnaise (egg). Dishes commonly come with sides like cream croquettes even on lighter plates, so dairy and egg are pervasive.

No information about allergy handling is documented. The shop is run by a single elderly chef with a small operation; diners with strict dietary needs should call ahead and confirm directly. Phone: 075-593-0054.
Cooking is done from scratch in-house, with handmade sauces, dressings, and mayonnaise, so the owner can speak directly to what goes into each dish if you ask.

name: やきとり雷 円町店 (Yakitori Kaminari – Enmachi)

claims.text: This is a charcoal yakitori grill. Tare-glazed skewers are brushed with a sweet soy-based sauce that contains wheat, and salt (shio) skewers, while sauce-free, are cooked on the same shared grill as the tare skewers. Cross-contact from shared grill surfaces and basting is likely. Not celiac-safe.

The tare (basting glaze) on yakitori is a soy-sauce-based sauce, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Tare-glazed skewers should be treated as containing wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce is documented here.

This is a chicken yakitori specialist with no documented vegan offerings; the menu centers on chicken skewers, and even vegetable items are cooked on a grill shared with meat. Not suitable for vegans.

Salt-grilled (shio) skewers are seasoned only with Hakata salt rather than the wheat-containing tare, so the seasoning itself is wheat-free - but they share the grill with tare skewers, so this does not make them celiac-safe. Confirm directly with staff.
